passage:
In the clinic waiting room, Amandeep slid the tablet into his bag. "Time's up, Chandrika. The doctor will call us soon."
Chandrika screamed, "No! It's mine! Five more minutes!" A few families glanced over.
"I hear you. You love that game," Amandeep said quietly. "The answer is still no. The tablet is finished for now."
"Five more minutes, please, please!"
"Not again. But you can pick a picture book from the shelf."
She kicked the chair leg, cried louder, then slowly took a book, tears still on her cheeks.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep put the tablet?
qa.a: He slid the tablet into his bag.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika scream when the tablet was put away?
qa.a: She felt something she loved was taken from her, and she hoped begging for five more minutes would bring it back.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do to keep the rule steady?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named her feeling, refused the extra minutes, and offered a book instead.

qa.q: What would change if Amandeep gave in to five more minutes?
qa.a: Chandrika would learn that screaming and begging works, so she would likely try it again next time.

grounding: A child shouts and cries when the parent turns off the tablet; the parent stays calm and keeps the rule without bargaining.

passage: The guests would arrive in ten minutes, and the house was a mess. Papa, Santosh, switched off the tablet. "Tablet time is over, Avni." Avni screamed. "No! Five more minutes!" Papa kept folding the sheets. "It's over. You can help me put flowers in the vase." "Five minutes! Please! Pleeease!" She cried and stamped. Papa was very tempted to say yes, just to get some quiet before the doorbell. But he didn't. "The answer is still no. I know you love that game." Avni sobbed on the sofa for a bit. Then she came and took a flower.

qa.q: What did Papa ask Avni to help with?
qa.a: He asked her to help him put flowers in the vase.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when the tablet was switched off?
qa.a: She felt robbed and upset, screaming and crying because she loved the game.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Santosh not to give in, even with guests coming?
qa.a: Giving five more minutes to stop the crying would teach Avni that crying works, so she would cry harder next time.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel as the doorbell time gets closer?
qa.a: He is likely stressed and tempted to give in for quiet, but he stays calm and firm.

grounding: A young girl shouts and cries when her parent turns off the tablet, and he stays calm and keeps the rule despite the pressure.

passage: In the flat above the bakery, Abbu, Imran, turned off the tablet at seven, like every night. Rehana howled. "It's MY game! You took it!" She threw a cushion. Imran picked it up and put it back. "I know. You love that game. Tablet time is finished." "Five more minutes!" "Not tonight." Rehana cried and bargained: "Two minutes? One?" Imran didn't argue. He sat on the floor with the storybook and began to read aloud about the grumpy crocodile. Rehana sobbed, then listened, then crept closer. "Why is he grumpy?" she asked.

qa.q: What time did Imran turn off the tablet?
qa.a: He turned it off at seven, like every night.

qa.q: What does Rehana throwing the cushion suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt angry and robbed of something she loved.

qa.q: What did Imran do instead of bargaining?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named that she loves the game, kept the rule and began reading a story nearby.

qa.q: How might Imran see Rehana's bargaining for fewer minutes?
qa.a: He sees that giving in once would teach her that crying and bargaining work, so he gently doesn't argue.

grounding: A young girl shouts and bargains when the tablet goes off, and her father stays calm, keeps the rule and offers a story.
